topic: Naive KV Caching OOMs Local Medical LLMs
postText:
Running local LLMs inside healthcare facilities is non-negotiable for strict patient data privacy. But the moment twenty medical staff query our on-prem clinical summary assistant concurrently, standard HuggingFace pipelines collapse with CUDA Out-Of-Memory errors.

The culprit is rarely model parameter size. It is the dynamic Key-Value (KV) cache.

Traditional inference pipelines allocate VRAM contiguously based on maximum context window length. When an electronic health record analysis uses 1,200 tokens but the engine pre-allocates for 8,192, over 70% of expensive GPU memory sits idle yet reserved. Under concurrent load, memory fragmentation instantly starves the hardware.

To stabilize our on-premise inference stack without tripling GPU spend, we transitioned to three core patterns:

1. PagedAttention: Operating system paging applied to VRAM. Splitting the KV cache into fixed-size physical blocks eliminates fragmentation down to sub-4% waste.
2. Continuous Token-Level Batching: Dynamic scheduling that injects new incoming prompts per forward pass rather than waiting for an entire batch of text generations to terminate.
3. AWQ (Activation-aware Weight Quantization): 4-bit weight compression protecting salient outlier channels so clinical diagnostic terminology retains near FP16 precision.

How do you handle the memory overhead of long context windows when deploying LLMs on local infrastructure? Do you prioritize aggressive quantization or virtualized KV caches?
